title: Accrual-Based and Real Earnings Management Activities Around Seasoned Equity Offerings

models.model_label: Year-1 matched-change ROA on discretionary accruals, sales growth and capex growth (Table 6 Panel A, column [6])
models.sample_description: Completed US seasoned equity offerings over 1987–2006 meeting the paper’s offer, issuer, data-availability, nonfinancial-firm, and earnings-management-measure criteria. In the post-SEO outcome, each issuer’s ROA change is adjusted by the ROA change of a size- and performance-matched nonissuing Compustat firm. Match candidates have prior-year-end assets within 90%–110% of the issuer; the candidate with the closest ROA is selected. The number of observations in each annual Table 6 regression is not reported.
models.method_reported: Fama–Macbeth regressions of DROA in years 1 to 3 on year 0 variables, estimated as annual cross-sectional regressions
models.method_details: Table 6 reports Fama–MacBeth coefficients and t-statistics from annual cross-sections. The paper does not identify the underlying estimator used within each cross-section.

fixed_effects.details: Table 6 reports annual cross-sectional regressions but does not report fixed-effect dummy families. Separate annual fits do not establish year fixed effects.

standard_errors.details: The reported Fama–MacBeth t-statistics summarize annual cross-sectional coefficient estimates.

evidence.quote: This table reports results of Fama–Macbeth regressions of DROA in years 1 to 3 on year 0 variables.

estimation_procedure.description: Estimate annual cross-sectional regressions and report time-series mean coefficients with Fama–MacBeth t-statistics. The dependent variable subtracts the ROA change of a matched nonissuer from the issuer’s ROA change. Candidate nonissuers are Compustat firms with no IPO or SEO during the sample period and with prior-year-end assets within 90%–110% of the issuer; choose the one whose ROA is closest in absolute terms.

evidence.quote: we estimate annual cross-sectional regressions
Nonissuing firms are those firms appearing in Compustat that did not make an initial public offering or seasoned equity offering in the sample period.
assets are within 90% and 110% of an issuer’s assets at the end of the fiscal year before the offering
we pick the one whose ROA is closest to that of the issuer in absolute terms

review_notes: The authors identify future operating performance as their third and most important contribution and specify the last, fully controlled Table 6 column in each panel. Earlier H1/H2 evidence, including Table 5 choice regressions, is outside this principal question.

missing_fields.method: The paper reports Fama–MacBeth results from annual cross-sections but does not name the underlying estimator within each cross-section.
missing_fields.sample_size: Table 6 does not report exact observation counts for each year-specific regression; the 1,511-offer sample total is not a per-fit N.

dependent_variable.name: DROA1
dependent_variable.definition: First difference in annual ROA in year 1 after the SEO, adjusted by subtracting the change in ROA of a size- and performance-matched nonissuing firm. ROA is income before extraordinary items divided by beginning-of-period total assets.

evidence.quote: The dependent variable, DROA, is computed as first difference in annual ROA, adjusted for the change in a size-matched and performance matched nonissuing firm ROA
where ROA is defined as income before extraordinary
items divided by beginning of period total assets
by subtracting the change in ROA of a size-matched and performance-matched nonissuing firm from the change in ROA of each issuing firm in years 1–3 following the SEO

independent_variables.name: Discretionary accruals
independent_variables.definition: Year-0 (SEO-year) discretionary accruals. DA is total accruals scaled by assets at t−1 less fitted normal accruals from Eq. (1). Total accruals are Compustat 123 earnings before extraordinary items and discontinued operations minus operating cash flows from continuing operations, Compustat 308 less 124. The normal-accrual fit uses the displayed scaled constant, change in revenue, and gross PPE, each divided by lagged assets.

evidence.quote: where our measure of discretionary accruals is the difference between total accruals and the fitted normal accruals
TAit =EBXIit

EBXI is the earnings before extraordinary items and discontinued operations (annual Compustat data item 123) and CFO is the operating cash flows (from continuing operations) taken from the statement of cash flows (annual Compustat data item 308 – annual Compustat data item 124).
Eq(1): TA_(i,t)/Assets_(i,t-1)=k1*(1/Assets_(i,t-1))+k2*(DeltaSALES_(i,t)/Assets_(i,t-1))+k3*(PPE_(i,t)/Assets_(i,t-1))+epsilon_(i,t).
Eq(2) predicted NA is the same three RHS terms with estimated coefficients.
total assets (annual Compustat data item 6)
DSALESit is the change in revenues (annual Compustat data item 12) from the preceding year
PPEit is the gross value of property, plant and equipment (annual Compustat data item 7).

sample_extraction.data_section_full_text:
3.1. Data and sample description


Our SEO sample consists of 1511 completed US offers over the 1987 to 2006 period, and is obtained from the Securities
Data Company (SDC) New Issue database. The sample criteria requires SEOs to be issues of common stocks by US issuers
that are listed on NYSE, NASDAQ, or AMEX and exclude the following: (1) SEOs lacking COMPUSTAT annual financial

ARTICLE IN PRESS

6 D.A. Cohen, P. Zarowin / Journal of Accounting and Economics 50 (2010) 2–19


statement data for the 4 years prior to the SEO filing date, the offer year and the subsequent year, (2) completed SEOs with
offer prices less than $5 and withdrawn SEOs with filing range midpoint less than $5, (3) spin-offs, (4) reverse LBOs, (5)
closed-end funds, unit investment trusts, REITS and limited partnerships, (6) rights and standby issues, (7) simultaneous or
combined offers of several classes of securities such as unit offers of stocks and warrants and, (8) nondomestic and
simultaneous domestic–international offers.

We collect our financial data from the COMPUSTAT annual industrial and research files for the sample period. We
restrict our sample to all nonfinancial firms with available data, and require at least 8 observations in each 2-digit SIC
grouping per year. Further, we require that each firm-year observation has the data necessary to calculate the discretionary
accruals metrics and real earnings management proxies we employ in our analysis. This restriction (used in other papers
on SEOs) likely introduces a survivorship bias into the sample resulting in the inclusion of larger and more successful firms.
We expect that this will reduce the variation in our earnings management metrics resulting in a more conservative test of
our research questions.

Following Collins and Hribar (2002), we use cash flows from operations obtained from the Statement of Cash Flows
reported under the Statement of Financial Accounting Standards no. 95 (SFAS no. 95, FASB 1987). <sup>4</sup> The sample period of
